text: ITSM Foundations taught you Standard, Normal, and Emergency changes as ITIL concepts. This lesson goes one level deeper — the real type field on change_request, and the distinct workflow path each type actually triggers once a real change record is created.

Standard changes are pre-authorized and need no individual approval. Normal changes get individually assessed and routed through approval. Emergency changes get an expedited authorization path — fewer approvers, but still a real one.

A Standard change is created from a Change Template — a pre-built record whose plan, risk, and affected Configuration Item were already reviewed once, at template-authorization time. Create a change from it, and it moves toward Scheduled and Implement with no new approval record, because re-approving a routine, repeatable action every single time would make the category pointless.

An Emergency change is not an unauthorized change. A well-implemented instance still requires real sign-off — typically from just one or two senior approvers, often a change manager or designated emergency-approval role — rather than the full chain a Normal change would route through. There isn't time to convene a board, but there is still a real, auditable approver accountable for the risk.

As the implementer, the practical question is: has this exact action already been pre-approved as a repeatable template, does every instance need its own assessment, or is it urgent enough to need a fast but still-real sign-off? Get this wrong and you either bury approvers in low-value repeat work, or let real risk slip through unreviewed as Standard.
Three types, three real paths, one field driving all of it. Next up: how risk actually gets assessed and calculated for a Normal change, instead of just guessed by whoever fills out the form.
